This hexagram brings success, but it carries a subtle teaching: the sun at midday is already beginning to set. Peaks don't last. The point isn't to be sad about that, but to shine fully while you're at the height. Make the most of the light. Use this moment to settle what needs settling, make clear decisions, and do the important things you can only do with this much energy and clarity. Abundance isn't something to cling to. It's something to use well while it's here.
judgment: Fullness, a peak moment of abundance and power. This brings success. Don't be sad that it won't last forever; be like the sun at noon, shining fully while it's at its height. Make the most of the light while you have it.
image: Thunder and lightning arrive together at the summit, power and clarity at once. Use a moment like this to settle what needs settling: make your judgments clear and act on them.
lineTexts: You meet someone who matches you, a partner equal in strength and clarity. Being alike in this way is no mistake. Spend this time together; it brings real progress. Going forward side by side, your energies amplify each other, and that is recognized and honored.

A screen has grown so thick that at midday you can see the stars. Something is blocking the light, and if you try to force your way to the people above you now, you'll meet suspicion and resentment. Instead, stay sincere and patient. Genuine conviction finds its way through in time, and brings good fortune.

Even darker now: a heavy curtain covers everything and only the faintest stars show at noon. You may lose the use of your strongest arm, unable to act on what you know. It isn't your fault. Wait it out; there is nothing to blame yourself for.

Still darkness at midday, the thick screen in place. But you meet someone who sees as you do, an ally of the same strength. Joining with them lets clarity return. Together you can see what neither could alone, and that brings good fortune.

Bringing capable, clear-sighted people around you. When you are open to talented help, the fullness of the moment becomes something shared and celebrated. This is a time for blessing and praise, and it brings good fortune.

Your house is grand, but it shuts everyone out. You peer through the gate and no one is there; for three years you see no one. Abundance turned into isolation is the danger of this line. Pride and walls bring misfortune. Open the door before the emptiness becomes permanent.
beneficial: A peak moment; shine fully and settle what needs settling.
beware: Peaks don't last; don't cling to the abundance, or waste it.
reflections: What is at its peak right now?
What could you settle while you have this energy?
How can you enjoy this without clinging to it?

label: Fire over Mountain
general: The traveler: away from home, in unfamiliar territory, without the usual support. This might be literal travel, a new job, a new community, or any time you're a stranger somewhere. On the road, you succeed through small things: courtesy, modesty, care, staying true to yourself. Don't make yourself conspicuous, don't get caught up in local conflicts, and don't overstay your welcome. Like a fire on a mountain that burns brightly and moves on, the traveler passes through. Go with an open heart but a clear mind. You may not belong here, but you can carry your integrity wherever you go.
judgment: The traveler, away from home, without a fixed place. On the road, you succeed through small things and modest conduct. Stay polite, careful, and true to yourself; don't make yourself conspicuous or overstay your welcome. That is how a wanderer finds good fortune.
image: A fire burns on the mountain, bright but quickly moving on. Be clear-eyed and careful when you judge others, and once a matter is settled, don't drag it out.
lineTexts: On the road, getting caught up in petty, trivial matters. Smallness and bickering invite trouble when you're a stranger. Keep your conduct dignified, even in small things. A traveler who wastes energy on petty concerns brings misfortune on themselves.

The traveler reaches an inn, carries what they need, and finds a loyal helper. You're secure for now: settled enough, with your resources intact and someone trustworthy at your side. Modesty and good sense have given you a safe place on the road.

The traveler's inn burns, and the loyal helper is lost. Arrogance or carelessness on the road has cost you your shelter and your support. Even if you're in the right, your position is now dangerous. Look honestly at how your own conduct played a part.

The traveler finds a resting place and has money and an axe to protect themselves, yet still says, 'My heart is not at ease.' You're safe enough, but not at home. That unease is natural for someone far from where they belong. It's not a sign anything is wrong, just a reminder that this is a stopover, not a destination.

You shoot a pheasant and lose the arrow at the first shot. A small price, but you hit your mark. Spending something to gain entry or recognition is worth it here. In the end, praise and a fitting position come to you.

The bird burns its own nest. The traveler laughs at first, then weeps and wails. Carelessness and arrogance have destroyed your shelter, and in a moment of thoughtlessness you have lost the patient steadiness, symbolized by a cow, that kept you safe. This brings misfortune. Humility on the road isn't optional.
beneficial: Courtesy and modesty make the journey smooth.
beware: Don't make yourself conspicuous or overstay your welcome.
reflections: Where are you a newcomer in this?
What would modesty look like here?
Which conflicts are not yours to join?

label: Wind over Wind
general: Gentle, persistent influence, like wind that finds its way into everything. This isn't about force but about steady, quiet pressure in one direction: repeated effort, patient persuasion, a soft voice that keeps speaking. That's how real change often happens. The hexagram brings success through small things. Have a clear goal, and keep working toward it gently. Seek out people who can guide you. Be flexible, but not aimless. Wind is gentle, yet over time it shapes mountains. Ask what you want to influence, and how you can bring it about through persistence rather than pressure.
judgment: Gentle, penetrating influence, the way wind works its way into every gap. Change comes through small, steady, persistent effort rather than force. It's good to have a clear direction now, and to seek out people who can guide you.
image: Wind follows wind, again and again, reaching everywhere. Repeat what matters until it takes hold: make your intentions clear, then follow through on them.
lineTexts: Going forward, falling back, unable to decide. Gentleness has turned into hesitation. What you need now is the decisiveness of a soldier: firm, clear and committed. Choose a direction and hold to it. That discipline will serve you well.

Searching beneath the bed, looking into hidden places to find what's wrong. Bring in people who can help uncover the hidden causes, the way the old text calls on priests and diviners. Patient, thorough searching brings good fortune and no blame.

Penetrating again and again, forcing it. Repeated, strained effort means you're overthinking or pushing too hard. Persistence has turned into compulsion, and that brings regret. Ease off. Gentle influence works through patience, not through brute repetition.

Regret disappears. On the hunt you catch game of three kinds, enough for every purpose. Your gentle, steady effort has paid off fully. This is a fruitful moment: action brings real results, and there is enough to share.

Persistence brings good fortune and regret falls away. Everything works out, though the start was rough. Before making a change, take three days to prepare; after it, three days to see how it lands. Careful preparation and careful review together make this succeed.

Searching beneath the bed again, but this time you've lost your axe, the very tool you need to act. Penetration has gone too far: so much probing and doubt that you've lost the power to decide. Even if you're right, this brings misfortune. Stop searching and recover your will.
beneficial: Gentle persistence succeeds where force would fail.
beware: Being flexible is good; being aimless isn't.
reflections: What do you want to change gently, over time?
Where could patience work better than pressure?
What direction would keep you focused?

label: Lake over Lake
general: Joy, openness, pleasure in life and in each other: two lakes side by side, refreshing each other. This hexagram brings success, as long as the joy is genuine. Real joy comes from inner steadiness and sincerity. It doesn't depend on flattery, indulgence, or empty pleasure. It's shared and warm, and it makes everything easier. Spend time with friends. Learn together, talk together. Joy multiplies when it's shared, and it gives energy to everything you do. Just be alert to joy that's hollow, or that comes at someone else's expense. True gladness feels clean.
judgment: Joy, open and shared, like light on the surface of a lake. This brings success, as long as the joy is genuine and steady, not empty pleasure or flattery. True happiness gives energy to everything you do.
image: Two lakes rest side by side, each refreshing the other. Share joy with friends in conversation and in learning together, so it keeps renewing itself.
lineTexts: Joy that comes from inner harmony, content and complete in itself. You don't need anything outside to feel glad, and you aren't chasing approval or distraction. This quiet, self-sufficient joy is the first and simplest kind, and it brings good fortune.

Joy that rests on sincerity. When your gladness is genuine and comes from a true heart, it can't be corrupted by temptations around you. Regret disappears. Stay honest in what you enjoy, and good fortune follows.

Joy chased from outside, pleasure pulled in from wherever you can find it. When you seek diversions to fill an emptiness inside, you lose yourself. This brings misfortune. Ask what you're really looking for under the hunger for pleasure.

Weighing up what to enjoy, unable to settle. You're torn between a higher joy and a lower one. Choose the higher and turn decisively away from what would harm you. Once you've chosen, there is real cause for gladness.

Trusting in something that is quietly wearing you down. A pleasant influence can be corrosive, and you're placing your confidence in it. This is dangerous. Be honest about who or what you're letting close, and guard against it.

Joy that leads you along, pleasure that draws you in. If you let yourself be pulled by every attraction, you lose your own direction. Notice what's leading you, and decide whether you really want to follow.
beneficial: Shared, genuine joy gives energy to everything you do.
beware: Hollow pleasure or flattery feels good but leaves you empty.
reflections: Where is there real joy here?
Who could you share it with?
Which pleasures might be empty?

label: Wind over Water
general: Things are dissolving, like ice melting on water. What had hardened, whether rigid attitudes, frozen relationships, or selfish divisions, is beginning to loosen. That can be good: it frees what was stuck. But dispersal can also scatter people and purpose. This hexagram asks you to gather people around something larger than themselves, something they can share. The old image is the king at the temple, uniting people through what they hold sacred. Find what connects you to others more deeply than your individual differences. It's a good time for great undertakings, especially those that bring people together. Let what's frozen melt, and let it flow toward something worth joining.
judgment: Things are coming apart, like ice melting on water. What has hardened, whether in your heart or between people, is softening. This brings success. It's a good time for something that draws people back together around what truly matters, and even a great undertaking is favorable.
image: Wind blows over the water, scattering what has frozen and set. When people are drifting apart, gather them around something larger than themselves, something they can share.
lineTexts: Bringing help while things are only beginning to scatter, with the strength of a good horse. Act early, before dispersal deepens and the problem hardens. A rift caught at the start is easy to mend. Swift, strong action now brings good fortune.

In the midst of things coming apart, hurry to what supports you. Find the steady ground, the people or practices that keep you whole, and lean on them. Regret disappears when you hold to what grounds you.
Letting go of your own self-interest. Dissolving the hard edges of ego for the sake of something larger isn't loss; it frees you. There's no regret in it. Give yourself to the work that needs doing.

Breaking up your own circle, setting aside narrow loyalties for a wider whole. This brings great good fortune. Out of the scattering, people gather again on higher ground, like a hill rising out of the plain. Most people wouldn't think of this; it takes vision to see it.

Like sweat breaking out in a fever, a great call goes out and dissolves what was stuck. Even someone in a high place gives away what they have stored up. A rallying idea and generous action pull people back together. There is no blame in this.

Dissolving what would bring bloodshed, going far away from danger. Removing yourself, and those you're responsible for, from harm isn't running away. It's wisdom, and sometimes the kindest thing you can do. There is no blame in leaving.
beneficial: What was frozen is melting; a good time to bring people together.
beware: Without a shared purpose, dispersal scatters people and plans.
reflections: What is starting to soften?
What could bring people back together?
What do you want to keep from drifting away?

label: Water over Lake
general: Limits give life its shape. Like the joints in bamboo, which make the stalk strong, the right boundaries create freedom rather than taking it away. This hexagram brings success. It asks you to set sensible limits on spending, time, energy, commitments, words. Know your capacity, the way a lake can only hold so much water. But it also warns against limits that are too harsh. If a rule is so strict that no one can live by it, it will break, and you'll end up worse off. Find the measure that's firm enough to hold you and gentle enough to bear. Moderation is its own kind of strength.
judgment: Limits, the boundaries that give life its shape. Like the joints of bamboo, they make strength possible. This brings success. But limits that are too harsh can't be sustained; if a rule chafes so badly that no one can live by it, it will break.
image: The lake can only hold so much water before it overflows. Measure things well: set clear standards for yourself, and reflect on what right conduct really means.
lineTexts: You don't step beyond the door into the courtyard. Knowing your limits and staying within them, at a time when going out would be premature, is right. Restraint and discretion keep you free of blame.

You don't step out through the gate when the time to go has come. Limits held too long, past their moment, become a trap rather than a protection. Hesitation now brings misfortune. When the opening appears, take it.

No limits at all, then lament. Without self-restraint, you overspend, overreach or overindulge, and you're left sighing at the consequences. You can't blame anyone but yourself. Accept it, learn the measure, and the regret can become a lesson.

Limits accepted calmly, held naturally without strain. When restraint feels right rather than forced, you can live by it easily, and it stops costing you effort. Measure has become part of who you are. This brings success.

Sweet limitation: limits that you live by first, that are easy and pleasant to follow. Leading by example rather than by command brings good fortune, because people follow willingly. Going forward this way earns respect and admiration.

Bitter limitation: harsh restrictions that no one can sustain. Persisting in them brings misfortune. Yet sometimes severity is necessary to protect what matters; if it truly is, regret will pass. Just don't mistake harshness for virtue.
beneficial: Sensible limits give you strength and freedom.
beware: Rules too harsh to live by will break.
reflections: What limit would make this stronger?
Which rule might be too strict?
How much can you really take on?

label: Wind over Lake
general: Inner truth: a sincerity so genuine it can reach even those who are hardest to reach. The old text says it can move even pigs and fish, creatures that don't respond to words. This hexagram is about the power of being real. When your heart is open and true, others feel it, and trust grows. It's a good time to undertake even difficult things. The image of wind moving over a lake suggests influence that works from within, stirring the deep water. It also asks for understanding toward others: try to see what's really in their hearts before you judge them. Sincerity, given and received, opens doors that persuasion can't.
judgment: Inner truth, a sincerity so deep it reaches even those hardest to reach, the way genuine trust can win over even the wariest creature. This brings good fortune, and even great undertakings go well now. Stay true at the center and others respond to it.
image: Wind moves across the lake, stirring the water's surface from within. Let that kind of understanding shape how you judge others: look for what's really there before you condemn, and be slow to pass final judgment.
lineTexts: Ready and grounded in yourself, at peace. Inner truth begins with steadiness that doesn't depend on others. If you look elsewhere for support or let hidden motives in, the calm is lost. Stay centered, and this brings good fortune.

A crane calls from the shadows, and its young answer. 'I have a good cup of wine; I'll share it with you.' Sincerity resonates on its own, without effort or display. Genuine feeling, quietly expressed, reaches those who are meant to hear it.

You find a companion, and now you drum, now you stop; now you weep, now you sing. When your center rests on someone else, your moods rise and fall with them. Notice the swings. Lasting steadiness has to come from within.

The moon is nearly full; the horse leaves its teammate behind. At your high point, turn away from partisan ties and look toward something higher. Letting go of a pairing that holds you back isn't disloyalty here. There is no blame in it.

Sincerity that binds people together, firm and true. Your inner truth links others to you as if hand in hand, without pressure or persuasion. This is the strength of real trust, and there is no blame in it.

A cockcrow trying to reach heaven. Words that claim more than the speaker can deliver. Sincerity that has turned into empty assertion rings hollow. Pushing it brings misfortune, even if your intentions are good. Return to what's real.
beneficial: Genuine sincerity builds trust and opens doors.
beware: Judge others hastily and you'll miss what's really in their hearts.
reflections: What would complete honesty look like here?
Whose heart might you be misreading?
Where could trust do more than persuasion?

label: Thunder over Mountain
general: A time for small things, done with extra care. Big plans and bold leaps won't work right now. The hexagram's image is a bird that should fly low, close to the ground, rather than try to soar. Stay humble and attentive to details. In your conduct, lean toward a little more respect, a little more care, a little more restraint than seems strictly necessary. Small steps, done well, bring good fortune. Reaching too high at this moment would be like a bird flying up into a storm. Do what's in front of you, carefully and well.
judgment: Small exceeding: a time when only small things can be done, and done carefully. Don't reach for great achievements now. Like a bird that should fly low rather than soar, stay close to the ground. Caution and humility bring good fortune.
image: Thunder on the mountain, a small sound carrying across the heights. In times like this, lean toward the modest: a little more respect than needed, a little more care, a little more restraint.
lineTexts: A bird tries to fly when it should still be in the nest. Overreaching before you're ready brings misfortune, and it comes fast. Wait until you're truly prepared. Stay low, build your strength, and remember that this isn't the moment to soar.

You pass by the ancestor and meet the ancestress; you don't reach the ruler but meet the official. You don't get to the top, but you meet the right person at your level. Accepting a modest route to your goal is no mistake.

Not taking extra precautions, and so someone comes from behind to strike. Overconfidence is dangerous now. Even if things seem secure, be more careful than you think you need to be. A little caution prevents real misfortune.

No blame. Meet the situation as it is, without overreaching. Going further would bring danger, so be on guard and don't press ahead. Don't be rigid about it either; this is a time to stay alert, flexible and modest.

Dense clouds but no rain from the western lands. A prince shoots and takes the bird in its cave. You can't accomplish the big things alone, but you can find the right helper, even someone hidden or overlooked. Look for them; they make the difference.

The bird flies past its mark, too high, too far. Overreaching to the extreme brings disaster that you've brought upon yourself. This is the danger of the whole hexagram. Come down to earth before it's too late.
beneficial: Small things done carefully bring good fortune.
beware: Reaching too high right now is like flying into a storm.
reflections: What small thing could you do well today?
Where might you be aiming too high right now?
What would a little more care change?

label: Water over Fire
general: Completion. Everything is in its place: every line in this hexagram sits in its proper position, like water over fire in perfect balance. Success has come. But completion is the most fragile of states. The hexagram warns that what begins well can end in disorder. Once things are finished, people relax and stop paying attention, and that's when things start to slip. Stay alert. Think ahead to what could go wrong and prepare for it now. Keep tending what you've built. Success is easier to achieve than to maintain. The real test of completion is what you do after it.
judgment: Things have come to completion, everything in its place, like water over fire in perfect balance. Success in small matters remains. But completion is fragile: things that start well can end in disorder if you stop paying attention. Stay watchful now that it's done.
image: Water sits above fire, the balance holding for now. Think ahead to what could go wrong, and prepare for it before it does.
lineTexts: Braking the wheels; the fox gets its tail wet. When everything has just been completed, a strong urge to keep moving forward can carry you too far. Hold yourself back a little. Restraint at this moment keeps you free of blame.

In the traditional image, a woman loses the curtain of her carriage and cannot travel. Something that let you move forward is gone for now. Don't chase it. In seven days, says the old text, it returns on its own. Patience costs nothing here.

An ancient king subdued a distant land, but it took three years. After completion, ambitions grow, and great undertakings are tempting. They take great effort and the right people. Don't give important tasks to those who aren't up to them.

Rags ready to plug the leaks in the boat, watchful all day long. Things are fine on the surface, but small cracks can open at any time. Stay alert and keep your remedies close at hand. Watchfulness now prevents trouble later.

The eastern neighbor sacrifices an ox; the western neighbor offers a small spring sacrifice, and receives the greater blessing. After success, elaborate display matters less than sincerity. A small, heartfelt act is worth more than a grand empty gesture.

Head in the water. Having made the crossing, you've gone back into it or turned around to look and are now submerged. Dwelling on what's done, or pushing past completion, is dangerous. Move on before you go under.
beneficial: Things are in place; success has come.
beware: Completion is fragile; relax your attention and disorder creeps in.
reflections: What is finished now?
Where might your attention slip?
What could go wrong next?

label: Fire over Water
general: Not yet complete. The I Ching ends here, not with completion but with the moment just before it. Things are moving toward order but haven't arrived; nothing is quite in its place yet. There's real promise, but also danger. The old image is a young fox crossing a frozen river, who gets its tail wet just before reaching the far bank. Carelessness at the end can undo everything. Go carefully, all the way. Take time to understand the situation and the pieces in it, so each can find its right place. And notice that the book ends on 'not yet' for a reason. Change never stops. Every ending is also a beginning.
judgment: Not yet complete, the moment just before the crossing is done. Success is possible, but like a young fox crossing the ice who gets its tail wet at the last step, carelessness at the end can undo everything. Go carefully all the way to the far bank.
image: Fire rises, water sinks, each still seeking its place. Before you act, take care to tell things apart clearly, so each can find where it truly belongs.
lineTexts: The fox gets its tail wet. Starting before the time is right, before you know how deep the water is, brings embarrassment. Rushing at the beginning of a crossing that isn't ready is a mistake that can be avoided.

Braking the wheels. You're ready to move, and the pull to go is strong, but restraining yourself for now is right. Your strength is better kept in reserve. Holding back, steady and true, until the moment arrives brings good fortune.

Not yet across. Pushing on without help or preparation would bring misfortune. Yet the moment calls for a bold crossing, if it's done the right way. Find a new approach or new allies, and the crossing becomes possible.

Perseverance brings good fortune, and regret falls away. Now is the time for a real effort, like an ancient campaign that took three years to win. The rewards are great, but they demand everything you have. Commit fully.

Steady and true, good fortune and no regret. The light of a wise person shines through. Sincerity makes the transition complete. This is the high point of the hexagram: the crossing succeeds, and it brings good fortune.

Celebrate with confidence, and there is no blame. But if you drink until your head is soaked, like a fox that gets its head wet, you lose what you've won. Enjoy the success, but stay aware. Don't let celebration turn into carelessness.
beneficial: The goal is in sight, and success is possible.
beware: Carelessness at the last step can undo everything.
reflections: How close are you to the finish, really?
Which last step needs the most care?
What still needs to fall into place?
